body:
What the reactivity series means

The reactivity series, also called the activity series, arranges metals in decreasing order of their tendency to react. A metal higher in the series is generally more reactive than one lower down.

The standard school-level sequence is:

Potassium > Sodium > Calcium > Magnesium > Aluminium > Zinc > Iron > Lead > Hydrogen > Copper > Mercury > Silver > Gold

Hydrogen appears in this sequence as a reference element, not because it is a metal. It helps predict whether a metal will displace hydrogen from ordinary dilute acids.

How displacement reactions work

A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive element replaces a less reactive element from its compound. In metal salt solutions, a metal higher in the reactivity series can generally displace a metal lower in the series.

The general relationship is:

More reactive metal + salt of less reactive metal → salt of more reactive metal + less reactive metal

Iron and copper sulphate

Iron is more reactive than copper. Therefore, iron can displace copper from copper sulphate solution:

Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu

The blue copper sulphate solution becomes greenish as iron(II) sulphate forms, and a reddish-brown deposit of copper appears on the iron.

The reverse reaction does not occur under ordinary conditions. Copper cannot displace iron from iron(II) sulphate solution because copper is less reactive than iron.

Zinc and iron sulphate

Zinc is more reactive than iron. Hence:

Zn + FeSO4 → ZnSO4 + Fe

By contrast, iron cannot displace zinc from zinc sulphate solution.

Using the same rule with silver

Copper lies above silver in the series. It can therefore displace silver from silver nitrate solution:

Cu + 2AgNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag

This comparison illustrates that a metal need not be near the top of the entire reactivity series to displace another metal. It needs to be more reactive than the particular metal present in the compound.

How hydrogen helps predict acid reactions

Metals such as magnesium, zinc and iron lie above hydrogen. They can displace hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid. Copper, silver and gold lie below hydrogen and do not ordinarily release hydrogen from these dilute acids.

This prediction does not mean that metals below hydrogen are chemically incapable of reacting with every acid. Oxidising acids can behave differently.

Reactivity and natural occurrence

Highly reactive metals readily combine with other elements and are generally found in nature as compounds. Less reactive metals, including gold and platinum, may occur in the native or uncombined state. Thus, reactivity also helps explain why different extraction methods are needed.

Prelims focus

  • The reactivity series is arranged in decreasing reactivity.
  • Zinc is more reactive than iron, and iron is more reactive than copper.
  • Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
  • Copper displaces silver from silver nitrate solution.
  • Hydrogen is a non-metal included as a reference point.
  • Trap: A less reactive metal cannot ordinarily displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.2.4–3.2.5, pp. 44–46; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 4, Materials: Metals and Non-Metals, pp. 50–52; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 6, Physical and Chemical Changes, pp. 60–62.]

pictures.caption: Common metals arranged from higher to lower reactivity.

title: The Reactivity Series and Displacement Reactions

body:
Electron transfer explains ionic bonding

Metal atoms commonly lose electrons during chemical reactions, forming positively charged ions called cations. Non-metal atoms commonly gain electrons, forming negatively charged ions called anions.

Oppositely charged ions attract one another. This electrostatic attraction is the basis of an ionic bond. Compounds formed through such bonding are called ionic compounds or electrovalent compounds.

Formation of sodium chloride

A sodium atom has atomic number 11 and electronic configuration 2,8,1. It has 1 electron in its outermost shell. By losing this electron, sodium obtains a stable outer shell and becomes a positively charged sodium ion, Na+.

A chlorine atom has atomic number 17 and electronic configuration 2,8,7. It needs 1 additional electron to complete its outermost shell. By gaining an electron, chlorine becomes a negatively charged chloride ion, Cl−.

In the formation of sodium chloride, sodium transfers an electron to chlorine. The resulting Na+ and Cl− ions attract each other.

The formula NaCl indicates equal numbers of sodium and chloride ions. Solid sodium chloride forms an extended arrangement of ions rather than existing as separate NaCl molecules.

Formation of magnesium chloride

Magnesium has atomic number 12 and electronic configuration 2,8,2. It loses 2 electrons to become Mg2+.

Each chlorine atom accepts 1 electron to become Cl−. Therefore, 2 chlorine atoms are needed to accept the 2 electrons lost by 1 magnesium atom.

The formula is MgCl2, consisting of Mg2+ and 2 Cl− ions in the required proportion.

The charges must balance. Na+ and Cl− combine in a 1:1 proportion, while Mg2+ and Cl− combine in a 1:2 proportion.

Properties of ionic compounds

Hardness and brittleness

Ionic compounds are generally hard crystalline solids because their oppositely charged ions are held together by strong attractive forces. However, they are also brittle: when sufficient force shifts layers in the crystal, repulsion between similarly charged ions can cause the crystal to break.

Melting and boiling points

Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points because considerable energy is required to overcome the attraction between their ions.

Solubility

Many common ionic compounds, such as sodium chloride, dissolve in water but do not dissolve in non-polar liquids such as kerosene. This is a general tendency, not a universal rule: some ionic compounds have very low solubility in water.

Electrical conductivity

Electrical conduction requires charged particles that can move. The key distinction is that the ions in a solid ionic compound are held in fixed positions.

ConditionMovement of ionsElectrical conduction
Solid ionic compoundIons cannot move freelyDoes not conduct appreciably
Molten ionic compoundIons can moveConducts
Aqueous ionic solutionDissolved ions can moveConducts when sufficient ions are present

A metal such as copper conducts electricity in the solid state because it contains mobile electrons. Solid sodium chloride does not conduct because its ions are fixed. Metallic conduction and ionic conduction have different charge carriers.

Prelims focus

  • Metals form cations by losing electrons; non-metals form anions by gaining electrons.
  • NaCl contains Na+ and Cl−.
  • MgCl2 contains Mg2+ and Cl− in a 1:2 proportion.
  • Ionic compounds are generally hard, brittle and high-melting.
  • Trap: An ionic compound may conduct when molten or dissolved, but not as a solid.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.3–3.3.1, pp. 46–49.]

pictures.alt: Sodium transfers 1 outer electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ whose opposite charges balance in NaCl.
pictures.caption: Sodium transfers 1 electron to chlorine, forming oppositely charged ions.

pictures.alt: Solid NaCl has fixed ions and barely conducts; molten NaCl and aqueous solutions conduct because their ions can move.

title: How Metals and Non-metals Form Ionic Compounds

body:
Why most metals must be extracted

Metals occur naturally in the Earth's crust in different forms. Some occur as uncombined elements, but many are present in chemical compounds. Whether a metal occurs freely or in a compound is closely related to its reactivity.

Highly reactive metals combine readily with oxygen, sulphur and other elements. Therefore, metals such as sodium, potassium, magnesium and aluminium are not ordinarily found as free elements in nature.

Less reactive metals such as gold and platinum may occur naturally in the native state, meaning an uncombined elemental form. Silver and copper may occur in both native and combined forms.

Mineral, ore and gangue

A mineral is a naturally occurring substance containing an element or its compound. An ore is a naturally occurring mineral or mineral-bearing material from which a metal can be extracted economically under the relevant conditions.

The distinction matters because a material may contain a metal without being a useful source for its extraction. If the metal content is too low or extraction costs are too high, the deposit may not be an economically useful ore.

Ores are usually mixed with unwanted substances such as soil, sand and rocky material. These impurities are called gangue.

Concentration or enrichment of ores

Before extracting the metal, much of the gangue is removed. This step is called concentration or enrichment of the ore.

Separation methods make use of differences between the ore and the impurities. Depending on the material, these differences may involve density, magnetic behaviour or other physical and chemical properties.

Concentration does not necessarily produce pure metal. It produces a material with a higher proportion of the desired metal-bearing substance, which can then undergo further extraction.

Examples of metal-bearing ores

MetalOre or compoundChemical formula
ZincZinc sulphideZnS
ZincZinc carbonateZnCO3
MercuryCinnabarHgS
CopperCopper sulphideCu2S

These examples also show why an ore may need chemical treatment. Zinc sulphide and zinc carbonate contain zinc, but neither is metallic zinc. Chemical reactions are needed to obtain the metal.

Occurrence and reactivity

The reactivity series helps explain natural occurrence:

  • Highly reactive metals: Usually present in compounds rather than in the native state.
  • Moderately reactive metals: Commonly occur in oxides, sulphides and carbonates.
  • Less reactive metals: May occur in the native state, although some also form ores.

This classification is a useful general guide rather than an absolute rule for every mineral deposit.

Prelims focus

  • All ores are mineral-bearing materials, but not all minerals are economically useful ores.
  • Gangue means unwanted earthy impurities associated with an ore.
  • Ore concentration removes gangue before metal extraction.
  • Gold and platinum may occur in the native state.
  • ZnS is zinc sulphide; ZnCO3 is zinc carbonate; HgS is cinnabar.
  • Trap: Concentrating an ore is not the same as obtaining pure metal.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.4–3.4.2, pp. 49–51; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 2, Is Matter Around Us Pure?, sections on mixtures and separation, pp. 14–20.]

pictures.alt: Concentration separates much of the unwanted gangue from mined material; the concentrated ore then needs chemical extraction to produce metal.
pictures.caption: Concentration removes gangue before chemical extraction.

title: Occurrence of Metals: Minerals, Ores and Gangue

body:
How reactivity determines the extraction method

Metallurgy includes obtaining metals from their ores and refining them for use. Extraction methods differ because metal compounds have different stabilities.

A highly reactive metal forms compounds from which the metal is difficult to obtain by ordinary chemical reduction. A less reactive metal can often be obtained more easily.

Reactivity groupExamplesSchool-level extraction approach
HighK, Na, Ca, Mg, AlElectrolytic reduction
ModerateZn, Fe, PbConversion to oxide followed by reduction
LowCu, Ag, AuNative occurrence or comparatively easier chemical extraction

This grouping explains the main principle. Specific ores and practical processes may differ, but the relationship between reactivity and ease of extraction remains central.

Roasting and calcination

Many moderately reactive metals occur as sulphides or carbonates. Their compounds are commonly converted into oxides before reduction because obtaining metal from an oxide is often easier.

Roasting

Roasting means heating a sulphide ore strongly in the presence of excess air or oxygen to convert it into an oxide.

For example, zinc sulphide forms zinc oxide and sulphur dioxide:

2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2

The sulphide is oxidised. The presence of oxygen is therefore an essential part of the reaction.

Calcination

Calcination involves heating an ore strongly in the absence or limited supply of air. Carbonate ores commonly decompose to form metal oxides and carbon dioxide.

For example:

ZnCO3 → ZnO + CO2

The important distinction is that roasting is associated with oxidation in excess air, whereas the decomposition of a carbonate during calcination does not require excess oxygen.

Reduction: obtaining the metal from its compound

Reduction, at this level, can be understood as removing oxygen from a metal oxide to obtain the metal. A substance that causes another substance to lose oxygen is acting as a reducing agent.

Carbon can reduce the oxides of certain moderately reactive metals. For example:

ZnO + C → Zn + CO

Zinc oxide loses oxygen and becomes zinc. Carbon combines with oxygen and forms carbon monoxide.

Highly reactive metals such as sodium, magnesium and aluminium cannot ordinarily be obtained from their oxides by heating with carbon because they have a stronger affinity for oxygen.

Electrolytic reduction of highly reactive metals

Electrolysis uses electrical energy to bring about a chemical change. Highly reactive metals are commonly extracted through electrolysis of suitable molten compounds.

For example, sodium can be obtained from molten sodium chloride. Positively charged sodium ions move towards the cathode, the negative electrode, where they gain electrons and form sodium metal. Chloride ions move towards the anode, the positive electrode, where chlorine is released.

Aluminium is obtained through electrolytic reduction of aluminium oxide. The precise industrial arrangement is beyond the present level; the essential principle is that electrical energy is used because ordinary carbon reduction is unsuitable.

The word molten is significant. The school-level example of sodium extraction uses molten sodium chloride, not an ordinary aqueous solution of common salt.

Extraction of less reactive metals

Some less reactive metals can be obtained from their oxides by heating. For example, cinnabar (HgS), an ore of mercury, is first converted into mercury oxide on heating in air. Further heating causes mercury oxide to decompose and release mercury.

Copper sulphide ores can also yield copper through suitable heating reactions. Gold and other very unreactive metals may occur naturally in the uncombined state.

Putting the stages together

The broad sequence is:

  1. Identify a suitable metal-bearing ore.
  2. Concentrate the ore by removing much of its gangue.
  3. Where necessary, convert sulphides or carbonates into oxides.
  4. Obtain the metal by an appropriate reduction or electrolysis process.
  5. Refine the impure metal when greater purity is required.

Prelims focus

  • Roasting: sulphide ore, excess air, usually forming an oxide.
  • Calcination: commonly carbonate ore, limited or absent air, often releasing CO2.
  • Reduction: obtaining metal by removing oxygen from its oxide.
  • Carbon can reduce some moderately reactive metal oxides.
  • Highly reactive metals commonly require electrolytic reduction.
  • Trap: Roasting, calcination, reduction and refining are different operations.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.4.2–3.4.5, pp. 50–52.]

pictures.caption: The broad extraction route depends on metal reactivity.
